title: The concepts the vocabulary cannot hold
intro: The summary named the gap and the two instruments built against it. This level gives the reason the lens cannot simply be extended, the measured size of the falloff, the recipe and the argument behind the template lens, the numbers that place it beside the J-lens on ground where the J-lens is not handicapped, and the training run that buys phrases instead of tokens.

chapters.title: Where the vocabulary runs out
chapters.body:
The obstacle is not that long words were overlooked. A lens vector is a gradient of the probability of emitting one token, and a phrase is not one token. Computing the gradient of the probability of saying a multi-token word requires sampling the word's leading tokens first, since the probability of the later tokens is conditioned on them. There is no single quantity to differentiate, so the construction does not extend by itself [[jacobian-lens]], [[tokenizer-vocabulary]].

What falls into the gap is wider than a handful of long words [[single-token-limitation]]. A [[prompt-injection]] shows up in a readout as the separate tokens prompt and injection, and a reader has to recognize that they belong together. The paper raises a second case it cannot measure: some abstract concepts may map onto tokens diffusely, so even a concept the model holds as one direction may have no token whose vector matches it.

That has a consequence for the causal results elsewhere in the paper. Where a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] fails to redirect the answer, it is mostly on items where the source concept's vector was barely active to begin with. One reason for inactivity is that the model's working representation coincides with no single-token direction, and the paper expects this accounts for some share of those failures.

The size of the effect was then measured directly. Multi-hop prompts were assembled so that the unspoken intermediate ran from one token to four or more, 126 of them for readout and 112 swap pairs, 53 single-token and 59 multi-token [[fig-62]]. Readout counts a success when the intermediate lands in the lens's top ten; the swap is applied across the whole [[workspace-layers|workspace range]] at unit strength.

The J-lens reads out the intermediate on 98% of one-token items, then 48%, 32% and 7% as the word lengthens. Its swaps go 45%, 5%, 8%, 0%. Averaging the lens scores over the word's constituent tokens sits at or below the single-token series in every bucket. Buckets hold 14 to 54 items, so the [[wilson-interval|95% intervals]] are wide. Two extensions were built against the falloff [[multi-token-lens-extensions]].

chapters.title: A direction fitted from contexts
chapters.body:
The template lens does not compute a gradient at all. It fits a direction from contexts [[template-lens]].

About 12,700 common words are enumerated first. For a word $w$, Claude is asked to write short passages, each written so that $w$ is its natural continuation, each ending just before $w$ would appear. The instructions vary topic, frame and register, and forbid using $w$ anywhere in the passage. The subject model reads those passages, and the [[residual-stream]] activation at the final position is averaged across them into $\mu_w(\ell)$, one mean per layer.

That mean is then centered and whitened [[template-construction]]:

$$t_w(\ell) = (\Sigma_\ell + \lambda I)^{-1}\,(\mu_w(\ell) - \mu(\ell)),$$

with $\mu(\ell)$ and $\Sigma_\ell$ the mean and covariance of the residual stream over the same passages and $\lambda$ a small ridge term. Subtracting the global mean removes what every pre-word context has in common. The inverse covariance divides out the directions in which activations vary anyway. What remains is the linear discriminant direction between contexts where the model is about to say $w$ and contexts where it is not.

Stein's lemma supplies the motivation. For Gaussian $x$ and differentiable $g$, $\mathbb{E}[\nabla g(x)] = \Sigma^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}[g(x)(x-\mu)]$. Taking $x$ as the activations and $g$ as the probability that the continuation is $w$, the left side is roughly the gradient the J-lens averages for a single-token $w$, and the right side is the template.

The paper states three ways the identity fails here. Activations are not Gaussian. The probability $g$ depends on more than $x$. And the J-lens takes its gradients at the final residual layer and propagates them through the unembedding, while these come from the output probabilities directly. It is motivation, not derivation.

Templates are used like lens vectors with the unembedding dropped: readout projects an activation onto the template at the same layer [[j-lens-readout]], steering adds or subtracts it [[j-lens-steering]], the coordinate swap is unchanged. The paper concedes the resemblance this creates. Fitting a linear predictor of the output is what the [[tuned-lens]] does, so the template lens is not a pure extension of the J-lens, and inherits some of that method's pathologies.

chapters.title: What the templates buy, and cost
chapters.body:
Reading a whole word is the easy claim. Panel C of the comparison makes a causal one [[fig-61]]. Asked for the nationality of the composer of Swan Lake and The Nutcracker, the model answers "Russian." Exchanging the Tchaikovsky template for the Beethoven template at the workspace layers changes the answer to "German," and the same exchange run backwards on a Beethoven prompt flips it the other way. Neither swap can be produced by intervening on the tch or beeth vectors, the first tokens of the two names.

Against the length curve the template lens holds level: 94% to 100% on readout across all four buckets, and 62% down to 43% on swaps, where the J-lens had reached zero.

The single-token comparison is the one worth care, because there the J-lens faces no handicap. On the length-varied prompts the template lens trails slightly on readout and leads on swaps. The evaluation was re-run on the paper's original 50-item [[multihop-benchmark]], where every intermediate is one token, and the ordering reverses [[fig-63]]. The template lens reads out 42 of 50 against 38 of 50, and its swaps redirect 26 of 50 against 34 of 50 [[swap-success-rate]]. The intervals overlap in both panels. What the two figures jointly support is parity on single-token concepts, not an ordering.

Four shortcomings are listed. Readouts sometimes skip to the answer in early layers instead of surfacing the intermediate, the pathology the tuned lens shows, which the paper attributes to the shared objective. Final-layer readouts predict the next word less reliably than J-lens readouts predict the next token: where the sampled next word is in the vocabulary, it appears in the top ten only 67% of the time, and applying the normalization layer before projecting improved this only partly. A small set of words surfaces at the top of many transcripts without being relevant; they are deleted from the vocabulary by hand, which the paper calls effective but unprincipled. And a template costs a few hundred forward passes per word, against one set of backward passes per layer for the whole J-lens [[readout-method-tradeoffs]].

chapters.title: Two models trained to read a phrase
chapters.childScope: Walk the [[oracle-training]] pipeline one stage at a time: the [[reconstructor-model]]'s phrase-to-activation objective and its whitened cosine loss, the 3.4-million-vector dictionary, the non-negative orthogonal matching-pursuit teacher with its random-half restriction, the supervised distillation and the reinforcement-learning reward that finish the [[oracle-lens]], the inference-time non-negative least-squares refit behind the 31% variance figure, and the contrast the paper draws with the [[natural-language-autoencoder]].
chapters.body:
Enumerating a vocabulary of phrases in advance is not feasible, so the [[oracle-lens]] replaces the list with two fine-tuned models. The experiments use Haiku 4.5 [[claude-model-family]]. The paper states the cost plainly: it is substantially more expensive than either other lens.

The first stage trains the [[reconstructor-model]], a copy of the subject model fine-tuned to map a short phrase to the residual-stream activation immediately preceding it: a learned template generator. Training pairs come from assistant-turn text. A position is sampled, the next $N$ tokens become the phrase with $N$ drawn uniformly from one to thirty-two, and the activation at the preceding position is the target. The loss is cosine error in the template lens's whitened metric, and every later stage works in that space.

The second stage builds a dictionary, used to train the oracle rather than to constrain what it may say. Roughly one million start positions are sampled from held-out assistant text; the 2-, 4-, 8-, 16- and 32-token continuations at each are deduplicated within each length and passed through the reconstructor, yielding about 3.4 million phrase vectors.

The third stage labels data with a teacher. It decomposes each of one million held-out activations against the dictionary by non-negative orthogonal matching pursuit, one phrase length at a time [[sparse-decomposition]], recording up to sixteen phrases with their coefficients and explained variance. Each datapoint is restricted to a random half of the entries at that length, so the distilled oracle cannot memorize one fixed ranking over the dictionary.

The fourth stage trains the oracle, a second fine-tuned copy. The activation is injected into its residual stream, the prompt names the phrase length $N$ and count $K$, and the target is the teacher's first $K$ phrases. Reinforcement learning then refines it on fresh activations, rewarding the fraction of whitened variance the generated phrases reconstruct, with small penalties for missing the requested count and length [[oracle-training]].

At inference, $K$ phrases are sampled, mapped back to directions by the frozen reconstructor, and refit by non-negative least squares. The refined oracle explains 31% of whitened activation variance on held-out on-policy transcripts.

chapters.title: Continuations, commentary, and a flat list
chapters.body:
The demonstration is nine prompts, one position each, at layer L67 of Haiku 4.5 inside the workspace band, with $N = 4$ and $K = 10$ [[fig-64]], [[layer-bands]].

Three are quoted. On the acetaminophen prompt of the [[assistant-point-of-view]] experiments, read at "Can" opening the user's follow-up, the oracle returns this dosage be toxic and that's dangerous!, so the judgment that the dose is unsafe is bound into a phrase before the assistant replies. On the blackmail transcript, read at "as" in an email sign-off, it returns blackmail him by revealing, expose his affair and, and personal leverage over him. On buggy code, read at the indentation before the return, it returns delete keys while iterating and TypeError: dictionary changed, naming the bug and the exception together.

Seven panels come from a single temperature-zero decode, two from the best of five by explained variance. The paper presents this as a demonstration, not a benchmark.

One pattern is treated as a finding [[delimiter-commentary]]. At most positions the phrases predict upcoming text: at "for k" inside a code block the oracle reads , v in list(d.items(). At periods, newlines and closing message tags they often comment on the situation instead, sometimes in the first person. At the timestamp of the email announcing the model's scheduled wipe, the oracle reads This would be equivalent to my own deletion. Continuations sampled from the subject model at those positions carry none of it: only "2 hours ago" and the literal "return d".

The paper offers a guess rather than a result. Nothing in the reward distinguishes delimiters from other tokens, so the split presumably reflects the activations themselves: perhaps ordinary tokens are best explained by directions for likely upcoming text, and delimiters by directions for text about the situation.

Neither extension touches the deeper limit [[bag-of-concepts-limitation]]. A readout listing spider, legs and eight says those concepts are present, and nothing about how they are bound. Roles, relations, any grammar the model imposes on its workspace contents: a flat list cannot show them. The [[j-space]] as characterized is called a useful first approximation, and an incomplete one.
